To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the service model is the most accurate model, (ii) the capacity model can be used when the service model is too complex, (iii) the inventory rule is a good approximation for the capacity model, and (iv) the fixed order size policy is the best policy.

(a) the proposed inventory rules perform well, (b) the proposed approximation models perform well for the considered problem, (c) the fixed order size policy performs well for the considered inventory system, and (d) the proposed inventory rule performs well for the multi-item system.

(1) for the capacity model the optimal solution can be found by using an inventory rule, (2) the service model can be solved by using a simple heuristic and (3) the performance of the (R, S) policy is comparable to the performance of the fixed order size replenishments policy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of inventory systems for point-of-use (POU) locations, which is an important problem in the health-care sector.
the development and evaluation of inventory control methods for hospitals.
the development of simple, exact and approximate models for point-of-use inventory management in hospitals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
(R, Q) policies with a simple inventory rule perform well for most of the inventory systems in hospitals.
the (R, S) policy is the best choice for the inventory control of point-of-use locations.
the (R, S) inventory policy is the best policy to use in a hospital department.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the (R, S) policy is a simple and effective way to control inventory at point-of-use locations.
the (R, S) policy performs well in a multi-item setting and that the (R) policy performs well when the service level is high.
the (R, S, s) policy is a good policy to use for the control of inventory in point-of-use locations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the (R, Q) policy is a good alternative to (S, s,1) policies in a hospital setting.
a simple (R, Q) policy can be used to control the inventory in a hospital department, and that the performance of the policy is close to that of a more complex inventory model with lost sales.
the capacity model and service model are both useful for inventory control of hospital departments.
